meta.abstract: Vistra Corp (VST, NYSE) is the Irving, Texas-headquartered integrated retail electricity and power generation company that emerged from the post-bankruptcy reorganisation of Texas Competitive Electric Holdings (a subsidiary of Energy Future Holdings) in October 2016 and was subsequently consolidated through the 2018 acquisition of Dynegy and the 2024 acquisition of Energy Harbor's nuclear and competitive power assets. The company operates approximately 41 gigawatts of generation capacity across ERCOT (Texas), PJM, MISO, and CAISO regions, with a fuel mix spanning natural gas (the largest single fuel by capacity), nuclear (Comanche Peak in Texas plus the Energy Harbor PJM fleet including Perry, Davis-Besse, Beaver Valley), coal, solar, battery storage, and adjacent renewables. CEO Jim Burke was named to the role in August 2022, succeeding Curt Morgan; Burke's prior role was Chief Operating Officer. The Energy Harbor acquisition in March 2024 for approximately $3.4 billion was the most consequential single transaction of the post-2022 period, adding approximately 4 gigawatts of PJM nuclear capacity and substantially expanding Vistra's contracted-revenue and PJM-capacity-market exposure. The retail electricity business under the TXU Energy and adjacent brand portfolio serves approximately 5 million customers across multiple deregulated US markets. Fiscal year 2025 (calendar year 2025) produced adjusted EBITDA in the approximate $5.5-6.5 billion range and adjusted free cash flow in the $3-4 billion range; revenue was in the $20+ billion range reflecting both the wholesale generation and the retail electricity supply businesses. The board is chaired by Scott Helm with directors carrying utility-industry, finance, and broader operational experience. The investment proposition compresses AI data centre electricity demand sustainability, the structural exposure to both ERCOT and PJM markets (geographic diversification beyond pure PJM nuclear peers like Talen and beyond pure ERCOT-anchored peers), the nuclear fleet positioning for hyperscaler PPAs (parallel to the Constellation Microsoft TMI and Talen Amazon Susquehanna transactions), and the integrated retail-wholesale business model that provides natural hedging across the wholesale-electricity-price cycle.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Vistra's hyperscaler contracting story developed in two stages. In August 2024, the company said it had completed two long-term renewable power purchase agreements totaling more than 600 MW: 200 MW with Amazon in Texas and 405 MW with Microsoft in Illinois. The disclosed nuclear contracts came later: a 20-year agreement with Amazon Web Services for up to 1,200 MW from Comanche Peak, with delivery expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027 and ramp to full quantity by 2032, and January 2026 20-year PPAs with Meta for 2,609 MW across Perry, Davis-Besse and Beaver Valley, including 433 MW of uprates. That chronology meant Vistra was not first into disclosed hyperscaler-nuclear contracting — Talen had already documented its March 2024 Susquehanna-AWS arrangement and Constellation signed Microsoft at Three Mile Island in September 2024 — but by early 2026 it had still assembled one of the larger merchant-nuclear corporate offtake books in the market [Vistra Q2 2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-08-08-Vistra-Reports-Second-Quarter-2024-Results) [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Vistra and Meta](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-01-09-Vistra-and-Meta-Announce-Agreements-to-Support-Nuclear-Plants-in-PJM-and-Add-New-Nuclear-Generation-to-the-Grid) [Talen SEC filing](https://ir.talenenergy.com/node/8961/html) [Constellation TMI-Microsoft](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/constellation-launch-crane-clean-energy-center-restoring-jobs/).

Vistra Corp ([VST, NYSE](https://investor.vistracorp.com/financial-information)) was headquartered in Irving, Texas, and at the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026 carried an equity market value of roughly $52.7 billion, based on the $156.27 closing price on 22 May 2026 and 337,182,468 shares outstanding as of 1 May 2026 [Vistra historical stock price](https://investor.vistracorp.com/index.php?s=125&ajax=ir_historical&date=2026-05-23&ticker=VST) [Vistra Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000014/vistra-20260331.htm). Jim Burke had served as President and Chief Executive Officer since 1 August 2022, while Kristopher Moldovan had served as Chief Financial Officer since 2022 [Vistra leadership](https://www.vistracorp.com/about/leadership/).

## Origin: Out of the Energy Future Holdings Estate

The company traced its lineage to the October 2016 emergence of Texas Competitive Electric Holdings — the unregulated generation and retail arm of Energy Future Holdings — from Chapter 11 bankruptcy. EFH had been created in the 2007 leveraged buyout of TXU Corporation by KKR, TPG, and Goldman Sachs, a roughly $44 billion transaction that subsequently buckled as shale gas re-priced the competitive generation stack. The post-reorganisation entity took the Vistra Energy name, retained the TXU Energy retail brand, and migrated to the NYSE in 2017. Burke's trajectory within the group — CEO of TXU Energy, then COO of Vistra, then President and CEO — reflected the company's integrated retail-plus-generation identity. Vistra, as of the snapshot date, was the clear number-two merchant generator behind post-Calpine Constellation rather than the largest operator outright: Vistra's 2025 Form 10-K listed 43,641 MW of total generation capacity and retail operations serving approximately 5 million customers across 16 states and the District of Columbia, including about 2.6 million Texas electricity customers under the TXU Energy brand [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Constellation completes Calpine](https://www.constellationenergy.com/newsroom/2026/01/constellation-completes-calpine-transaction-powering-americas-clean-energy-future.html).

## The Energy Harbor Transformation

Vistra announced the acquisition of Energy Harbor Corp on 6 March 2023 and closed the transaction on 1 March 2024 for total consideration of approximately $3.43 billion: roughly $3.0 billion in cash, assumption of approximately $430 million in Energy Harbor debt, and a 15 percent equity stake in Vistra Vision — the Vistra subsidiary housing the combined nuclear and renewables portfolio — transferred to Energy Harbor's prior stakeholders. The acquired fleet comprised 4,048 MW of nuclear generation at Davis-Besse, Perry and Beaver Valley, taking Vistra's nuclear portfolio from 2,400 MW at Comanche Peak to 6,448 MW across four sites. Energy Harbor also contributed approximately one million retail customers. Vistra later bought back the outside stake in Vistra Vision on 31 December 2024, restoring full ownership of the nuclear-and-clean-energy vehicle [Vistra completes Energy Harbor](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-03-01-Vistra-Completes-Energy-Harbor-Acquisition) [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results).

## The Hyperscaler PPA Cascade

The 2024 renewable PPAs proved a precursor rather than the opening nuclear move. In 2025 Vistra disclosed the AWS Comanche Peak PPA; in January 2026 it followed with the Meta agreements, under which Meta agreed to buy 2,176 MW of operating energy and capacity from Perry and Davis-Besse plus 433 MW of uprates across Perry, Davis-Besse and Beaver Valley. Management said the AWS contract could begin delivering in late 2027 and ramp to full quantity by 2032, while Meta's operating volumes were expected to begin in late 2026 and reach full delivery by year-end 2027, with uprates running out to 2034 [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Vistra and Meta](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-01-09-Vistra-and-Meta-Announce-Agreements-to-Support-Nuclear-Plants-in-PJM-and-Add-New-Nuclear-Generation-to-the-Grid).

> "This commitment from Meta provides Vistra the certainty needed to invest in these plants and communities and bring new nuclear generation online for the grid." — Jim Burke, January 2026

## Financial Re-Rating

The earnings trajectory captured the structural shift. Vistra reported Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA of $4.140 billion in 2023, $5.656 billion in 2024 and $5.912 billion in 2025; operating revenues were $14.779 billion, $17.224 billion and $17.738 billion respectively. The 2024 step-up reflected ten months of Energy Harbor ownership and the recognition of estimated nuclear production tax credits, while 2025 added the first full post-close year plus two months of Lotus ownership [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results) [Vistra FY2025 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-02-26-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Results).

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Adj. EBITDA (Ongoing Ops.) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | $14.779B | $4.140B | [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results) |
| 2024 | $17.224B | $5.656B | [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results) |
| 2025 | $17.738B | $5.912B | [Vistra FY2025 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-02-26-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Results) |

> "I am proud of the 2025 performance of our Vistra team — this was truly a transformational year for our company." — Jim Burke, February 2026

Management guided fiscal 2026 Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA of $6.8 billion to $7.6 billion and Ongoing Operations Adjusted FCFbG of $3.925 billion to $4.725 billion; as of 1 May 2026 it said it had hedged about 98 percent of expected generation volumes for 2026, 89 percent for 2027 and 65 percent for 2028 [Vistra Q1 2026 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-05-07-Vistra-Reports-First-Quarter-2026-Results).

## Moss Landing: Battery Storage in the Dock

On 16 January 2025, Vistra detected a fire at the Moss Landing 300 MW energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant site in Monterey County, forcing it to cease operations across the complex until the fire was contained. In later filings the company said the Moss Landing 300 MW and 100 MW battery facilities would not return to service, while the separate 350 MW battery facility remained under evaluation for a possible mid-2026 restart pending completion of the cause investigation; the gas plant returned to service in February 2025. Insurance recovery, environmental remediation and other incident expenses were still being worked through inside the frozen window [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Vistra Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000014/vistra-20260331.htm).

The fire raised systemic questions about lithium-ion battery safety at utility scale in densely populated coastal locations — questions that Vistra's nuclear and gas acquisitions had not posed.

## Central Questions

At the snapshot date, Vistra traded as a Texas-anchored merchant power franchise with disclosed hyperscaler exposure across both renewable and nuclear assets: 605 MW of solar PPAs with Amazon and Microsoft, plus 3,809 MW of nuclear PPAs with AWS and Meta. Three questions framed the analysis ahead. First, having shown it could contract Comanche Peak and the PJM fleet, could Vistra extend that framework to its gas fleet, and at what carbon-intensity discount or premium? Second, after Constellation's January 2026 completion of Calpine, how did Vistra's 43.6 GW portfolio compete against a 55 GW rival with far greater nuclear depth? Third, what did Moss Landing — and the capital it continued to absorb — imply about the pace and risk tolerance of Vistra's storage ambitions relative to the gas-and-nuclear cash engine that funded them [Vistra Q2 2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-08-08-Vistra-Reports-Second-Quarter-2024-Results) [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Constellation completes Calpine](https://www.constellationenergy.com/newsroom/2026/01/constellation-completes-calpine-transaction-powering-americas-clean-energy-future.html).

chapters.title: From Energy Future Holdings Chapter 11 to the Energy Harbor acquisition
chapters.body:
## The integrated utility and the leveraged bet

Before the private-equity era, TXU Corporation was the defining integrated electric utility of deregulated Texas — a sprawling holding company that combined rate-regulated wires assets, merchant generation, and the state's largest retail electricity franchise. Its competitive generation arm, weighted heavily toward coal-fired baseload capacity in ERCOT, operated under the logic that Texas population growth would drive sustained power demand and that whoever owned the baseload plant would capture the price upside.

In October 2007, that thesis attracted what was then the largest leveraged buyout in history. A consortium led by KKR and TPG Capital, with Goldman Sachs' private equity arm as a significant co-investor, acquired TXU Corporation for approximately $44 billion — a transaction that loaded the surviving entity, renamed Energy Future Holdings, with roughly $40 billion of debt. EFH was reorganised into three principal subsidiaries: Texas Competitive Electric Holdings (TCEH), which held the competitive generation fleet and TXU Energy retail; Luminant, the generation operating company; and Oncor Electric Delivery, the regulated transmission and distribution utility.

The financial bet was directional: natural gas prices would remain elevated or rise, preserving the implied margin for coal-fired generation that was priced against gas at the margin in ERCOT. It was, in retrospect, one of the more expensive single-variable errors in private-equity history.

## The shale revolution and the Chapter 11

The Barnett Shale had already begun producing in volume when the EFH deal closed. By 2009 the Haynesville and Marcellus plays were flooding the US gas market with supply that permanently restructured the price curve. Henry Hub spot prices, which had spiked above $13 per MMBtu in mid-2008, collapsed below $2 by April 2012. In ERCOT — a power market that sets its marginal price against gas-fired generation — lower gas prices meant lower wholesale electricity prices, which meant structurally impaired merchant margins for Luminant's coal-heavy fleet.

Energy Future Holdings, carrying its LBO debt load against a deteriorating margin environment, entered creditor restructuring negotiations in 2013. In April 2014 the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware — at the time one of the largest corporate bankruptcies in US history by debt quantum. The filing separated EFH's regulated and competitive businesses along structural lines embedded in the original acquisition architecture. Oncor Electric Delivery, ring-fenced from the competitive businesses, proceeded through a separate sales process that ultimately brought the regulated T&D asset to Sempra Energy. TCEH — the competitive generation and retail vehicle — pursued its own reorganisation track.

## The birth of Vistra Energy

In October 2016, TCEH emerged from bankruptcy as a standalone competitive generation and retail company, renamed Vistra Energy. TCEH's senior secured creditors received equity in the newly-formed entity as their reorganisation recovery — a structure that delivered a disciplined capital table to the post-bankruptcy vehicle, unburdened by the debt architecture that had sunk EFH. Vistra Energy initially traded over-the-counter before graduating to the New York Stock Exchange in 2017 under the ticker VST.

What emerged was a merchant power pure-play: Vistra retained the Luminant generation brand across coal, gas, and nuclear assets in ERCOT; the TXU Energy retail brand, which was the largest competitive retail electricity provider in Texas; and, critically, Comanche Peak — the two-unit, 2.4-gigawatt pressurised-water nuclear plant in Somervell County, Texas, that would later anchor Vistra's nuclear contracting strategy with hyperscaler customers. The post-bankruptcy management team, led by Chief Executive Curt Morgan, moved quickly to establish Vistra as a disciplined capital allocator: debt was retired, share buybacks were executed, and the operational focus shifted to free cash flow from the existing fleet.

## The Dynegy acquisition and the PJM foothold

In April 2018, Vistra completed the acquisition of Dynegy — a rival competitive power generator with a multi-regional fleet spanning PJM, MISO, ISO-NE, and NYISO — in an all-stock transaction that valued Dynegy's equity at approximately $1.7 billion, with Vistra assuming Dynegy's outstanding debt in addition. The combined company cleared approximately 38 gigawatts of generation capacity, roughly doubling Vistra's footprint and diversifying it across five regional transmission organisations.

The strategic logic was consolidation at distressed valuations. Vistra at emergence was ERCOT-concentrated with limited presence outside Texas; Dynegy brought PJM and MISO capacity — gas-fired combined-cycle and peaker plants, plus legacy coal assets undergoing retirement — that established Vistra as a multi-regional merchant operator. The Dynegy integration also established the template for the subsequent Energy Harbor transaction: acquire a creditor-controlled competitive generation asset at a price set through restructuring process rather than a contested strategic auction, absorb the operational and commercial infrastructure, and generate synergies from procurement, commercial optimisation, and capital structure rationalisation.

## The Burke succession and the IRA tailwind

In August 2022, Curt Morgan retired as Chief Executive after leading Vistra through post-bankruptcy emergence, the Dynegy integration, and the extraordinary market conditions of Winter Storm Uri in February 2021. James A. Burke — who had served as Chief Operating Officer and had earlier led TXU Energy as its Chief Executive — succeeded him on 1 August 2022.

The timing was consequential. Seventeen days later, President Biden signed the Inflation Reduction Act into law on 16 August 2022. The IRA's Section 45U Production Tax Credit established a zero-emissions electricity production credit for existing nuclear generation, creating a floor price mechanism that materially improved the forward cash flow profile of Vistra's Comanche Peak asset. For merchant nuclear operators running fully dispatchable, high-capacity-factor generation, the 45U PTC converted a portion of nuclear value from market-price exposure to an indexed federal credit, reducing cash flow volatility and sharpening the investment thesis for fleet expansion.

Burke's strategic thesis — nuclear as the backbone of grid reliability and AI data centre power supply — was already visible in Vistra's capital allocation before the Energy Harbor announcement.

## Energy Harbor: The nuclear transformation

On 6 March 2023, Vistra announced the acquisition of Energy Harbor Corporation — a competitive nuclear and retail power company formed from the 2020 bankruptcy reorganisation of FirstEnergy Solutions — for total consideration of approximately $3.43 billion. The deal structure combined approximately $3.0 billion in cash, assumption of approximately $430 million of Energy Harbor debt, and a 15% equity stake in a newly-created Vistra subsidiary, Vistra Vision, which would consolidate the acquired Energy Harbor nuclear assets alongside the existing Comanche Peak plant and Vistra's broader renewables and storage portfolio.

The four reactors acquired were Davis-Besse (a single-unit pressurised-water reactor in Ottawa County, Ohio), Perry (a single-unit boiling-water reactor in Lake County, Ohio), and Beaver Valley Units 1 and 2 (pressurised-water reactors in Beaver County, Pennsylvania) — together adding 4,048 megawatts of PJM nuclear capacity [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm). The acquisition transferred approximately one million retail electricity customers in PJM competitive markets alongside the four reactors, meaningfully expanding Vistra's retail franchise outside Texas.

Burke, announcing the transaction in March 2023, described it as transformative — establishing Vistra as the nation's largest competitive power producer and positioning the company as the second-largest operator of nuclear capacity in the United States. Kristopher Moldovan, Vistra's Chief Financial Officer, characterised the deal's financial structure as capital-efficient given the 45U PTC floor and the PJM capacity market pricing environment. The transaction closed on 1 March 2024, following Nuclear Regulatory Commission and Federal Trade Commission clearances.

The Energy Harbor close transformed Vistra's nuclear positioning from a single 2.4-gigawatt Texas plant to a 6.4-gigawatt fleet spanning three states. Within PJM — where the July 2024 capacity auction cleared at prices that surprised even bullish market participants, reflecting structural capacity scarcity across the region — the four Energy Harbor reactors commanded premium values in both energy and capacity markets.

## What the post-bankruptcy era produced

Across eight years from the October 2016 emergence, Vistra's evolution followed a consistent arc: bankruptcy reorganisation delivered a disciplined capital structure; the Dynegy acquisition added multi-regional scale; the IRA reshaped the nuclear economics; and Energy Harbor transformed a Texas-focused merchant generator into one of the largest competitive power producers in the United States by installed capacity.

| Metric | FY 2022 | FY 2023 | FY 2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue (USD bn) | 13.728 | 14.779 | 17.224 |
| Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) | 3.115 | 4.140 | 5.656 |
| Nuclear capacity (GW) | 2.4 | 2.4 | 6.4 |
| Total generation capacity (GW, approx.) | ~38 | ~38 | ~41 |

Vistra exited 2024 as a roughly 41-gigawatt operator carrying 6.4 gigawatts of nuclear capacity, approximately five million retail customers across deregulated US markets, two newly disclosed renewable PPAs with Amazon and Microsoft, and a management team publicly signalling larger-load discussions across the expanded nuclear fleet. The disclosed nuclear PPAs with AWS and Meta came later, outside the historical period covered in this chapter. The trajectory from TCEH creditor recovery vehicle to principal Texas-anchored AI power play was, by any measure, among the more improbable reinventions in the history of US competitive electricity.

chapters.title: Generation by region, TXU retail, and the Vistra Vision subsidiary
chapters.body:
## Five Regional Footprints, One Retail Anchor

In its 2025 annual report, filed inside the frozen window, Vistra described a 43,641-MW generation fleet and retail operations serving approximately 5 million customers across 16 states and the District of Columbia. That scale reflected not only the March 2024 Energy Harbor acquisition but also the November 2025 Lotus closing, which added 2,557 MW of gas-fired capacity. Full-year 2025 operating revenues were $17.738 billion and Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA was $5.912 billion [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Vistra FY2025 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-02-26-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Results).

## ERCOT: The Texas Foundation

Texas remained the largest single region in Vistra's portfolio, and ERCOT's structural characteristics made it the most consequential one for earnings trajectory. Vistra's Texas footprint centred on the 2.4 GW Comanche Peak nuclear station in Glen Rose — two units, Unit 1 and Unit 2, operating at consistently high capacity factors — supplemented by a substantial fleet of natural gas combined-cycle plants and peaking units distributed across ERCOT's four weather zones.

ERCOT's design as an energy-only market, without a centralised capacity mechanism of the type used in PJM, meant that scarcity pricing events — when system-wide supply margins tightened and the nodal price approached or reached the market cap — could generate disproportionate revenue in short, concentrated intervals. The operating reserve demand curve, which Vistra's executives frequently referenced in earnings discussions as a structural feature favouring dispatchable generation, served to monetise capacity scarcity directly into energy prices rather than through a separate auction. Texas's emergence as the preferred landing zone for US AI data centre development — driven by low land costs, proximity to large power infrastructure, and a permitting environment markedly faster than northeastern and Pacific states — strained ERCOT load forecasts materially through 2024 and into 2025, with the Electric Reliability Council of Texas revising its interconnection queue demand estimates upward multiple times over the period.

Comanche Peak sat at the centre of Vistra's commercial strategy in ERCOT. As a baseload nuclear plant qualified for the IRA Section 45U production tax credit, Comanche Peak's economics carried a government-provided floor. The July 2024 licence renewal through 2050 and 2053, and the later 20-year AWS nuclear PPA disclosed in 2025, turned the plant from a pure merchant baseload asset into a partially contracted nuclear platform [Vistra Comanche Peak renewal](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-07-30-Vistra-Receives-Approval-to-Operate-Comanche-Peak-Nuclear-Plant-Through-2053) [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm).

## PJM: The Energy Harbor Transformation

Prior to the March 2024 Energy Harbor close (see Corporate History for deal terms), Vistra's PJM footprint was modest. The acquisition added 4,048 MW of dispatchable zero-carbon baseload capacity, bringing total nuclear to approximately 6.4 GW across four sites. The July 2024 PJM capacity auction, which cleared at $269.92/MW-day across most of the RTO footprint, meant the acquired reactors captured a materially different capacity-revenue backdrop almost immediately [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [PJM](https://insidelines.pjm.com/pjm-capacity-auction-procures-sufficient-resources-to-meet-rto-reliability-requirement/).

|---|---|---|---|
| Comanche Peak Unit 1 | Glen Rose, TX | 1,200 MW | ERCOT |
| Comanche Peak Unit 2 | Glen Rose, TX | 1,200 MW | ERCOT |
| Davis-Besse | Oak Harbor, OH | 908 MW | PJM |
| Perry | Perry, OH | 1,268 MW | PJM |
| Beaver Valley Unit 1 | Shippingport, PA | 939 MW | PJM |
| Beaver Valley Unit 2 | Shippingport, PA | 933 MW | PJM |
| **Total nuclear** |  | **6,448 MW** |  |

*Source: [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm)*

Energy Harbor also brought approximately one million retail customers in PJM-overlapping competitive retail markets, broadening Vistra's retail presence beyond Texas for the first time at material scale.

## MISO, NYISO, and ISO-NE: Secondary Positions

Outside of ERCOT and PJM, Vistra operated natural gas and, in diminishing quantities, coal-fired assets across the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO), the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), and ISO New England (ISO-NE). These three regions collectively represented a smaller share of total segment contribution than ERCOT or PJM, and the company's coal fleet across MISO in particular was subject to an active retirement schedule — reflecting the combined pressure of age, tightening environmental compliance costs, and natural gas and renewable economics that persistently undercut economic dispatch. Vistra's strategy in the secondary regions leaned toward holding dispatchable gas assets where capacity market participation or ancillary service revenues justified continued operation, while systematically exiting coal positions where the retirement economics were more attractive than continued operation.

## TXU Energy and the Retail Franchise

TXU Energy, the retail electricity brand Vistra inherited from the TCEH bankruptcy estate, provided retail electricity to approximately 2.6 million customers in Texas as of 31 December 2025, while Vistra's retail operations overall served approximately 5 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across 16 states and the District of Columbia [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm). Texas's deregulated electricity market — covering roughly 85 percent of the state's load and served by competitive retail providers operating over a common distribution infrastructure — had been Vistra's largest single source of operating cash flow contribution for most of its post-bankruptcy history. The retail business functioned as a natural hedge against the wholesale generation portfolio: when ERCOT wholesale prices rose sharply on scarcity events, the generation segment captured premium revenues, while the retail segment faced cost pressure unless pass-through mechanisms or fixed-price contract mixes absorbed the increase.

Vistra supplemented TXU Energy's primarily Texas-residential focus with Ambit Energy, a multi-state direct-sales retail brand acquired in 2019, and additional competitive retail brands serving commercial and industrial customers in deregulated markets beyond Texas. The combined retail customer count, inclusive of the PJM-region customers added through Energy Harbor, positioned Vistra as one of the largest competitive retail electricity providers in the United States by customer count.

The retail business carried a structurally different financial profile than the generation segment: relatively capital-light, operationally intensive at the customer acquisition and billing layer, and sensitive to customer churn rates and the competitive dynamics of a Texas retail market where hundreds of licensed providers competed on price comparison platforms. Management historically characterised the retail franchise as a strategic anchor — its predictable cash flows offsetting the earnings volatility inherent in merchant generation — rather than a high-growth vehicle.

## Vistra Vision: The Nuclear-and-Clean Subsidiary

The March 2024 Energy Harbor acquisition gave rise to a new entity in Vistra's corporate structure: Vistra Vision, the vehicle designated to hold the combined nuclear fleet (Comanche Peak plus the four Energy Harbor reactors), the renewables portfolio, and the battery storage assets. Energy Harbor's former stakeholders initially received a 15 percent equity stake in Vistra Vision as part of the transaction consideration, but Vistra repurchased that minority interest on 31 December 2024 and by the frozen window again owned 100 percent of the vehicle [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results).

That repurchase simplified the corporate structure without eliminating the strategic optionality. Vistra Vision still concentrated the zero-carbon fleet, renewables and storage in one place, preserving optionality for future financings or a carve-out even though no such transaction had been announced by the snapshot date [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results) [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm).

## Battery Storage: DeCordova and the Vistra Vision Portfolio

Vistra Vision's portfolio extended beyond nuclear to encompass the company's battery storage footprint. The 260 MW DeCordova battery energy storage system in Texas remained one of the larger standalone battery installations in ERCOT, while the California picture had changed abruptly after the January 2025 Moss Landing fire: Vistra later said the Moss Landing 300 MW and 100 MW battery facilities would not return to service, while the separate 350 MW battery facility remained under evaluation for a possible mid-2026 restart [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Vistra Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000014/vistra-20260331.htm).

## Segment Revenue Profile

Vistra reported consolidated operating revenue of $17.224 billion in fiscal 2024, against $14.779 billion in 2023 and $13.728 billion in 2022. The step-up from 2023 to 2024 reflected both the acquisition close on 1 March 2024 — meaning fiscal 2024 captured roughly ten months of Energy Harbor contribution — and continued ERCOT wholesale price uplift.

| Fiscal year | Revenue (USD bn) | Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 13.728 | 3.115 |
| 2023 | 14.779 | 4.140 |
| 2024 | 17.224 | 5.656 |

*Sources: [Vistra FY2022 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2023-03-01-Vistra-Reports-Full-Year-2022-Results), [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results)*

The adjusted EBITDA expansion from $4.140 billion in 2023 to $5.656 billion in 2024 — a $1.516 billion increase, or 36.6 percent growth — reflected the combined effect of Energy Harbor's nuclear contribution, the elevated PJM capacity auction clearing, and estimated nuclear production tax-credit revenue. The two 2024 renewable PPAs, and then the later AWS and Meta nuclear contracts, were what turned that improved earnings base into a more durable market narrative [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results) [Vistra FY2025 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-02-26-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Results) [Vistra and Meta](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-01-09-Vistra-and-Meta-Announce-Agreements-to-Support-Nuclear-Plants-in-PJM-and-Add-New-Nuclear-Generation-to-the-Grid).

chapters.title: $17.2B revenue, $5.7B adjusted EBITDA, and the Energy Harbor accretion
chapters.body:
## The 2024 Earnings Step-Change

Vistra Corp closed fiscal year 2024 with operating revenue of $17.224 billion and Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA of $5.656 billion — figures that marked the most consequential earnings inflection in the company's post-bankruptcy history. The 2024 EBITDA figure represented a 36.6 percent expansion over the $4.140 billion recorded in fiscal 2023, and sat 81.6 percent above the $3.115 billion produced in 2022. Three forces converged to generate that step-change: the March 2024 close of the Energy Harbor acquisition, structural capacity scarcity in ERCOT, and a broad repricing of PJM capacity market revenues that the company's newly enlarged nuclear fleet was positioned to capture [Vistra FY2022 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2023-03-01-Vistra-Reports-Full-Year-2022-Results) [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results).

The revenue trajectory over the three-year window told a story of compounding scale. Vistra moved from $13.728 billion in 2022 to $14.779 billion in 2023 before the $17.224 billion 2024 total absorbed roughly ten months of Energy Harbor's contribution. The company entered 2025 with a materially different earnings base than the one Jim Burke inherited when he assumed the CEO role in August 2022 — and by the end of 2025, after the Lotus acquisition, total generation capacity had risen to 43,641 MW [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results) [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm).

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) | EBITDA Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 13.728 | 3.115 | 22.7% |
| 2023 | 14.779 | 4.140 | 28.0% |
| 2024 | 17.224 | 5.656 | 32.8% |

## The Energy Harbor Accretion Engine

The financial arithmetic of the Energy Harbor acquisition (see Corporate History for deal terms) became clearer in the twelve months following the March 2024 close. Vistra Vision ringfenced nuclear and clean-energy assets into a subsidiary that initially carried an external 15 percent equity stake as part of the consideration package. That structure reflected a bilateral view that the nuclear fleet — valued with IRA Section 45U tailwinds and AI-cycle optionality — warranted a different valuation frame from Vistra's merchant gas and retail operations. By 31 December 2024, however, Vistra had repurchased the minority interest and once again wholly owned the vehicle [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results).

## Section 45U and the Nuclear Earnings Floor

The IRA's Section 45U production tax credit provides a per-megawatt-hour subsidy for zero-emission nuclear generation that phases down as wholesale prices rise but establishes an effective floor when prices fall. At a 95 percent capacity factor, a 6.448 GW fleet would produce roughly 53.7 terawatt-hours annually. The structural effect is an earnings floor that did not exist pre-IRA: in low-price environments the credit cushions cash flow; in high-price environments the operating leverage remains visible in EBITDA [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm).

## PJM Capacity Market Repricing

The July 2024 PJM capacity auction for the 2025-2026 delivery year cleared at $269.92 per megawatt-day across most of the footprint — a dramatic repricing from the deeply suppressed levels that had characterised PJM capacity markets for much of the prior decade. PJM itself linked the result to generator retirements outpacing additions and to accelerating data-centre and broader load growth [PJM](https://insidelines.pjm.com/pjm-capacity-auction-procures-sufficient-resources-to-meet-rto-reliability-requirement/).

For Vistra, the PJM repricing translated into substantial incremental capacity revenue for the Energy Harbor reactors — revenue streams that were largely absent from the pre-acquisition Vistra financial model, which had been heavily ERCOT-anchored. At $269.92/MW-day applied across 4,048 MW of acquired nuclear capacity, the order-of-magnitude annualised gross capacity value approached $400 million before any locational adjustments, helping explain why the Energy Harbor purchase looked materially more accretive after the auction than it had at signing [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [PJM](https://insidelines.pjm.com/pjm-capacity-auction-procures-sufficient-resources-to-meet-rto-reliability-requirement/).

The PJM repricing also illustrated the structural asymmetry in Vistra's post-acquisition positioning. Where Vistra pre-2024 was principally exposed to ERCOT energy market dynamics — highly volatile, capacity-market-light, and acutely sensitive to Texas weather patterns — the Energy Harbor acquisition diversified that exposure into PJM's structured capacity framework, where multi-year clearing prices provide more visible forward earnings than ERCOT's energy-only construct.

## ERCOT Scarcity and the AI Data Centre Premium

Vistra's ERCOT footprint remained the engine of the gas-and-retail earnings stack through 2024. The operating reserve demand curve converted periods of thin reserves into abrupt price spikes during summer peak-load events, allowing the fleet to monetise scarcity directly in the energy market rather than through a separate capacity construct.

The structural driver beneath those episodic scarcity events was the accelerating build-out of AI data centre capacity in North Texas. The Dallas-Fort Worth corridor had emerged as the largest US market for hyperscaler computing investment by square footage, driven by a combination of permissive interconnection timelines, an available labour pool, and the commercial attractiveness of Texas's competitive power market. ERCOT's own load forecasts, revised upward through 2024, incorporated the data centre demand surge, suggesting that structural tightening — not simply weather-driven variability — would characterise the ERCOT balance through the end of the decade.

Vistra's position within that dynamic was straightforward: as the largest generator by installed capacity in ERCOT, with a gas peaker and combined-cycle fleet capable of capturing scarcity pricing, and with the Comanche Peak nuclear plant operating as an uncorrelated must-run baseload, the company sat at the intersection of two premium pricing regimes simultaneously: scarcity rents during stress events, and the structural load growth that was compressing ERCOT's reserve margins.

## The AWS Comanche Peak PPA

Vistra did not publicly disclose a nuclear hyperscaler PPA in 2024. The first disclosed nuclear contract came later, when management said in February 2026 that the company had signed a 20-year agreement with AWS for up to 1,200 MW of carbon-free power from Comanche Peak, with delivery expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027 and ramp to full quantity by 2032. The commercial significance was the same one the market had been anticipating earlier: part of Comanche Peak's output would be converted from merchant exposure into contracted cash flow while leaving the broader fleet available for further bilateral structuring [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Vistra FY2025 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-02-26-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Results).

## Capital Allocation: Buybacks and Debt Management

Vistra's capital allocation through the 2024 earnings cycle reflected the confidence of a management team operating with a materially expanded free cash flow profile. The company maintained an active share repurchase programme — one of the more aggressive return-of-capital postures among US independent power producers — alongside a dividend that was modest in absolute terms relative to the buyback scale [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results) [Vistra FY2025 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-02-26-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Results).

The Energy Harbor financing added to the long-term debt stack, and debt management — balancing the incremental leverage from the acquisition against the expanded EBITDA base — became a focal point of investor communication through 2024. The constructive story held through the frozen window: 2025 Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA rose again to $5.912 billion even before any contribution from the announced Cogentrix acquisition.

## Moss Landing: The Battery Storage Exception

The January 2025 Moss Landing fire (see Snapshot) introduced a discrete variable into the accretion story. Vistra's later filings made clear that the incident centred on the 300 MW battery facility, that the 300 MW and 100 MW battery systems would not return to service, and that the separate 350 MW battery facility was still being evaluated for restart. In the context of a nearly $6 billion EBITDA base, the earnings significance remained contained; the larger consequence was to the market's view of utility-scale storage risk [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm) [Vistra Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000014/vistra-20260331.htm).

chapters.title: From the 2022 Burke succession to the 2024 Energy Harbor inflection
chapters.body:
## The Burke Era Begins: August 2022

Burke assumed the CEO role from Curt Morgan on August 1, 2022 (see Corporate History for background). The succession came seventeen days before the IRA was signed into law. His strategic inheritance was substantial: a multi-market generation fleet of roughly 38 GW, retail operations that already reached into the millions of customers, but only a single 2.4 GW nuclear plant at Comanche Peak. Fiscal 2022 produced $3.115 billion of Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA against $13.728 billion of operating revenue.

## The Energy Harbor Announcement: March 2023

The March 2023 announcement (see Corporate History for deal terms) marked the most consequential merchant-power acquisition of the post-IRA era. The Section 45U dynamic provided a revenue floor that de-risked the economics substantially. Fiscal 2023 produced $4.140 billion of Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA against $14.779 billion of operating revenue — the market beginning to price IRA clarity, tightening ERCOT margins, and a much more valuable nuclear optionality set.

## Energy Harbor Close, Renewable PPAs, and Licence Renewal: 2024

The Energy Harbor acquisition closed on 1 March 2024, transforming Vistra's nuclear fleet from a single plant to a 6.4 GW, six-reactor, three-state platform. The next disclosed hyperscaler steps in 2024 were not nuclear PPAs but the August announcements of 200 MW and 405 MW renewable PPAs with Amazon and Microsoft respectively, followed within weeks by the NRC approval extending Comanche Peak's operating licences through 2050 and 2053. Those moves made the later nuclear contracts more financeable even before the AWS and Meta agreements were disclosed [Vistra Q2 2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-08-08-Vistra-Reports-Second-Quarter-2024-Results) [Vistra Comanche Peak renewal](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-07-30-Vistra-Receives-Approval-to-Operate-Comanche-Peak-Nuclear-Plant-Through-2053).

## ERCOT Scarcity and PJM Repricing: H2 2024

The second half of 2024 delivered the capacity-pricing catalyst. PJM's July 2024 auction cleared at $269.92/MW-day, translating directly into revenue visibility for Vistra's 4,048 MW of acquired PJM nuclear capacity. Full-year 2024 results confirmed the earnings expansion: $17.224 billion of revenue and $5.656 billion of Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA — an 81.6 percent increase versus fiscal 2022 [PJM](https://insidelines.pjm.com/pjm-capacity-auction-procures-sufficient-resources-to-meet-rto-reliability-requirement/) [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results).

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 13.728 | 3.115 |
| 2023 | 14.779 | 4.140 |
| 2024 | 17.224 | 5.656 |

*Source: Vistra Corp investor filings; SEC EDGAR CIK 0001692819*

VST shares, alongside Constellation Energy's CEG, emerged as among the best-performing US large-cap equities of 2024-2025. The re-rating dynamic was principally AI-driven: the equity market revised its long-run power demand assumptions materially upward as hyperscaler capital expenditure guidance from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta indicated data centre build programmes measured in hundreds of billions of dollars over multi-year horizons. Zero-carbon, firm generation capacity — nuclear, in particular — traded at a structural premium within this framework, and Vistra's 6.4 gigawatt nuclear fleet, bracketed by the IRA PTC floor and increasingly collateralised by long-dated hyperscaler offtake, sat at the intersection of every relevant demand vector.

## Moss Landing and the Battery Storage Reassessment: January 2025

The January 2025 Moss Landing fire (see Snapshot) introduced a risk variable not fully priced into the merchant storage thesis. Management's response balanced immediate insurance recovery against broader questions about lithium-ion safety management across the storage fleet.

## The Hyperscaler PPA Pipeline: 2025 and Beyond

Through 2025 and into 2026, the hyperscaler pipeline expanded from the 2024 renewable PPAs to the first disclosed nuclear contracts: the AWS Comanche Peak agreement and the Meta PJM agreements. Burke's consistent message was disciplined capital allocation. The IRA Section 45U floor provided downside protection; the hyperscaler demand queue provided commercial leverage; and Moldovan emphasised the growing proportion of earnings that was contracted, PTC-protected, or capacity-market-secured [Vistra FY2025 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-02-26-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Results) [Vistra and Meta](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-01-09-Vistra-and-Meta-Announce-Agreements-to-Support-Nuclear-Plants-in-PJM-and-Add-New-Nuclear-Generation-to-the-Grid).

The earnings story from the August 2022 succession through the first quarter of 2026 was, at its core, the story of a timely strategic bet executed with disciplined capital-structure management. Burke inherited a platform built for Texas energy-market scale; he extended it into PJM nuclear through the Energy Harbor acquisition, used the 2024 renewable PPAs and Comanche Peak relicensing to establish a contracting template, and by 2025-2026 had converted that template into disclosed AWS and Meta nuclear agreements. The AI-cycle re-rating of merchant nuclear was the macro tailwind. The execution — the IRA structuring through Vistra Vision, the PJM capacity-auction timing, the Vision minority buy-in, and the later hyperscaler PPA origination — was the operating story underneath it.

chapters.title: Burke, Moldovan, the Vistra Vision team, and the post-EFH board
chapters.body:
## The Morgan-to-Burke succession and the arc of operating continuity

On August 1, 2022, James A. Burke was named President and Chief Executive Officer of Vistra Corp, succeeding Curtis Morgan. Morgan had served as founding CEO from the company's emergence from the Energy Future Holdings Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2016 through six years of institutional rebuild: the 2018 Dynegy acquisition that doubled Vistra's generation footprint across PJM, MISO, and New York, the catastrophic stress-test of Winter Storm Uri in February 2021, and the early framing of what would become the most durable power-price re-rating cycle in ERCOT's history. When Morgan stepped back, the board did not recruit externally. It promoted the executive who had spent the preceding six years as COO absorbing the Dynegy integration and running the generation fleet alongside the retail operation — and who, before that, had spent eleven years running the retail business itself.

Burke joined TXU Energy — the competitive retail electricity subsidiary that survived the EFH bankruptcy and became the consumer franchise anchoring Vistra's integrated model — in 2004. By 2005 he was Chairman and Chief Executive of TXU Energy, a role he held for eleven years through the EFH period, the bankruptcy, and the post-emergence restructuring. That retail tenure is the foundation of his institutional authority: TXU Energy serves approximately five million residential and business customers in Texas, competing against dozens of rival retail electric providers in the ERCOT open market, and generates the stable margin that underwrites the company's merchant-generation volatility. Burke understands the retail electricity business at granular depth — customer acquisition economics, churn and lifetime-value modelling, hedging programme design, the regulatory interface with the Public Utility Commission of Texas, and the competitive dynamics of a market where consumers can switch providers online in minutes.

When Vistra emerged from bankruptcy in October 2016, Burke transitioned from TXU Energy CEO to Chief Operating Officer of the parent company, a deliberate broadening move that placed him in direct oversight of the wholesale generation fleet. He held the COO portfolio from 2016 to 2020, absorbing the Dynegy integration and the management of a generation mix that spanned natural gas combined-cycle units, legacy coal assets under a retirement programme, the battery storage build-out, and the two-unit Comanche Peak nuclear facility in Glen Rose, Texas. In 2020 he was elevated to President and Chief Financial Officer — an unusual dual portfolio that combined balance-sheet stewardship with operating authority — before the August 2022 CEO succession.

His educational formation is atypical for a large-cap merchant power CEO: a Bachelor of Arts in Economics and an MBA in Finance from Tulane University, followed by both a CPA certification and a CFA designation — the latter a financial-markets credential more common among investment analysts than industrial operators. He subsequently completed an MIT Nuclear Reactor Technology course, a substantive signal of personal commitment to the nuclear asset category that by 2024 would represent more than a third of Vistra's installed capacity. Burke sits on the board of the Nuclear Energy Institute, Washington's principal nuclear power trade association, and on the Tulane Energy Institute's advisory board.

## Kristopher Moldovan: the CFO as balance-sheet architect

Kristopher Moldovan has been Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer since 2022, though his institutional roots at the company trace to 2006 — a decade before the CIK 0001692819 corporate entity existed. His early career followed an engineering-then-law trajectory: a Bachelor of Science in Engineering from the University of Illinois, followed by a law degree from Duke and practice at Gibson, Dunn and Crutcher and Wildman, Harrold, Allen and Dixon, before an in-house move to what was then a predecessor entity of Vistra, where he joined as Senior Counsel. He subsequently added a finance certificate from SMU's Cox School of Business.

The career arc matters because the CFO's command of structured transactions, credit agreement mechanics, and hedging instrument documentation is built on primary professional formation rather than delegated review. His treasury progression — Assistant Treasurer from 2010 to 2017, then SVP and Treasurer from 2017 to 2022 — gave him direct ownership of the liability side of the balance sheet through the most consequential episodes in the company's post-EFH history. The Energy Harbor financing in 2024 tested that capability at scale: Vistra funded approximately $3.4 billion in cash consideration while absorbing roughly $430 million of Energy Harbor's existing debt and issuing a 15 percent equity stake to Energy Harbor stakeholders — all without triggering a ratings downgrade or a dilutive equity offering. The transaction closed March 1, 2024. On subsequent earnings calls, Moldovan's capital allocation commentary — structured around adjusted EBITDA guidance ranges, free cash flow before growth conversion, and the pace of the share repurchase programme — reflects the treasurer's instinct for cash mechanics that accounting earnings can obscure.

## The C-suite: strategy, law, retail, and public affairs

Stacey Doré holds the title of Executive Vice President, Chief Strategy and Sustainability Officer, and Head of Public Affairs — a portfolio spanning M&A origination, regulatory engagement, external communications, and the ESG reporting function. Her formation is lawyerly: she began at Vinson and Elkins, the Houston firm that has served as institutional counsel to the Texas energy industry for generations, before moving in-house to InfraREIT as SVP and General Counsel and subsequently to Hunt Utility Services and its regulated-transmission subsidiary Sharyland Utilities as CEO. The Sharyland operating experience — a Texas transmission utility serving rural ERCOT territory under regulated cost-of-service economics — is a genuinely different commercial model from Vistra's merchant-generation core and provided rare CEO-level exposure to the infrastructure and regulatory side of the electricity system. Doré sits on the Williams Companies board, providing current exposure to the natural gas midstream sector increasingly entangled with power-market dynamics.

Stephanie Zapata Moore serves as EVP and General Counsel, having come through the Luminant generation subsidiary — Vistra's Texas-based fossil and nuclear generation operating company — where she served as VP and General Counsel before elevation to the corporate role. Her practice background at Gardere Wynne Sewell encompassed corporate and securities work alongside trial practice, a combination relevant to a company that operates in contested regulatory environments and whose commercial positions in wholesale markets generate ongoing counterparty and regulatory litigation exposure.

Scott Hudson leads the retail operation as President of Vistra Retail, overseeing TXU Energy and the company's competitive retail portfolio across sixteen states. Hudson's background is non-traditional: he trained as a commercial lawyer at Troutman Sanders before roles at MBNA America, ChoicePoint, and LexisNexis — businesses built on customer identification, data analytics, and credit risk — before joining TXU Energy in 2011. The analytical toolkit for a competitive retail electricity business is closer to financial services than to generation operations: customer acquisition cost optimisation, lifetime-value modelling, churn prediction, and price-to-beat positioning in a market with real-time switching. Hudson's background aligns that toolkit directly.

The government affairs function is led by Sano Blocker, SVP of Government Affairs, who has been with the company and its predecessor entities since 2008, holding the equivalent role at Energy Future Holdings before carrying it through the bankruptcy emergence into the Vistra structure. His continuity through the EFH restructuring and the post-emergence period builds an institutional memory of legislative and regulatory dynamics — at the PUCT, the Texas Legislature, the NRC, and in Washington on IRA implementation — that an externally recruited government affairs head would require years to replicate.

## Nuclear governance: Vistra Vision and the Energy Harbor inheritance

Vistra Vision, the subsidiary established to hold the company's nuclear generation assets, carries dual institutional lineage: the legacy Comanche Peak operations team built under TXU and then Vistra ownership in Glen Rose, Texas, and the Energy Harbor nuclear organisation that operated Davis-Besse and Perry in Ohio and Beaver Valley 1 and 2 in Pennsylvania. The board-level governance of the nuclear business is anchored by John W. ("Bill") Pitesa, who joined the Vistra board in 2024 concurrent with the March Energy Harbor acquisition closing and chairs the board's Generation and Safety Oversight Committee.

Pitesa's career in the nuclear industry spans more than forty years: he served as Chief Nuclear Officer at Duke Energy — one of the largest nuclear operators in the United States — before serving as Chief Nuclear Officer of the Nuclear Energy Institute, the same trade body on whose board Jim Burke sits as a current member. Before the acquisition closed, Pitesa had chaired the nuclear safety and oversight committee of Energy Harbor's own board. His appointment to the Vistra board at the moment of the acquisition's closing was a deliberate governance decision: it brought the Energy Harbor nuclear committee chair directly into the combined entity's board-level nuclear oversight structure, providing continuity of safety governance through what is always a challenging integration period for nuclear operations.

## The board: post-bankruptcy composition calibrated for merchant power

Scott Helm has chaired the Vistra board since 2017. His career began at Goldman Sachs in fixed income and investment banking before he became EVP and Chief Financial Officer of Orion Power Holdings, a merchant power generator active in the competitive-market build-out of the early 2000s. He was subsequently a founding partner of Energy Capital Partners, the energy-focused private equity firm. The ECP founding role is the thread that explains his Chairmanship: Energy Capital Partners was a significant participant in the EFH restructuring and Vistra's emergence from Chapter 11, and Helm's position as Chairman reflects the governance continuity from that creditor-to-equity-holder transition.

Gavin Baiera has been on the board since 2016 — the bankruptcy emergence year itself — as Senior Managing Director and Partner at Centerbridge Partners, the multi-strategy private investment firm that was among the distressed-credit holders of EFH and TCEH debt through the restructuring. Baiera previously ran Strategic Finance at Morgan Stanley and was a Managing Director at Angelo, Gordon and Co., making him a structurally sophisticated voice on Vistra's capital structure, hedging programme, and capital allocation decisions.

Paul Barbas joined in 2018 through the Dynegy acquisition, which brought Dynegy's independent directors into the combined company's board. He is a former President and CEO of DPL Inc., the holding company for Ohio utility Dayton Power and Light, and held EVP-level operating roles at Chesapeake Utilities and Allegheny Power. J.R. Sult, also a Dynegy-acquisition director and the Audit Committee chair since 2018, is a career CFO: EVP and CFO of Marathon Oil, EVP and CFO of El Paso Corporation, VP and Controller at Halliburton Energy Services, and earlier an audit partner at Arthur Andersen. The Dynegy pair provides peer-utility operating challenge and financial-reporting-grade audit governance simultaneously.

Lisa Crutchfield chairs the Social Responsibility and Compensation Committee and brings regulatory authority experience that is rare at the board level: she served as Vice Chairman of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission in the early 1990s before senior executive roles at National Grid as EVP and Chief Regulatory, Risk and Compliance Officer, at PECO (an Exelon subsidiary) as SVP of Regulatory Affairs, and at Duke Energy as VP of Energy Policy. The PJM-geography regulatory depth — Pennsylvania in particular — maps directly onto the Energy Harbor nuclear assets operating within PJM's footprint.

Hilary Ackermann chairs the Sustainability and Risk Committee. Her final role at Goldman Sachs was as Chief Risk Officer of Goldman Sachs Bank USA, overseeing the bank's market, credit, and counterparty risk frameworks. That formation — systematic quantification of commodity price exposure, counterparty default risk, and tail risk — maps onto the principal financial risk the Vistra equity story carries: unhedged power price volatility in ERCOT and PJM is the variable that drives the equity return over any given twelve-month period.

Julie Lagacy has chaired the Nominating and Governance Committee since 2023. She spent the bulk of her career at Caterpillar across finance, HR, global information services (as CIO), and enterprise strategy, ending as Chief Sustainability and Strategy Officer. Her industrial-CFO background and cybersecurity governance training address the operational technology and information security risk exposure of a company running nuclear plants, gas-fired generation, and a large retail electricity trading platform under the same corporate roof.

Rob Walters joined the board in 2024 — again concurrent with the Energy Harbor closing — having retired from Gibson, Dunn and Crutcher in 2023 after serving on the firm's worldwide executive committee. Before his final chapter at Gibson Dunn, Walters had served as EVP and General Counsel of Energy Future Holdings Corp. His presence provides what no external director search could manufacture: institutional memory of the EFH structure, its regulatory history in Texas, and the commercial relationships that predated Vistra's 2016 emergence, combined with four decades of outside-counsel perspective on the electric power sector.

Arcilia Acosta has been on the board since 2020. She is CEO of CARCON Industries and Construction and founder and CEO of Southwestern Testing Laboratories, both Texas-based enterprises. She served on the Energy Future Holdings board for a decade, providing predecessor-entity governance continuity, and chaired the Dallas Citizens Council in 2023 and 2024. Her Texas civic and business presence is relevant to the regulatory and community relations dimensions of the company's continued ERCOT presence.

The resulting composition — a Goldman-and-ECP founding partner as Chairman, a Centerbridge distressed-credit investor as the longest-tenured independent director, two Dynegy-acquisition executives providing utility-CEO and CFO-grade challenge, a forty-year nuclear industry veteran anchoring nuclear safety governance, a former Pennsylvania PUC regulator overseeing compensation, a Goldman risk officer overseeing commodity risk, and a former EFH General Counsel providing predecessor-entity institutional memory — is explicitly calibrated for the post-bankruptcy merchant-power-plus-competitive-retail operating model Vistra runs. It is not the board of a regulated utility with a guaranteed rate of return. It is the board of a company whose equity return is shaped, quarter by quarter, by the price of power at the ERCOT North hub at peak demand hours and by the PJM capacity market's willingness to price scarcity.

chapters.title: Microsoft, hyperscalers, TXU retail customers, and the gas-and-uranium supply chain
chapters.body:
## The Hyperscaler Turn

When Jim Burke stepped back to assess Vistra's 2024 results in the company's February 2025 earnings release, he reached for a phrase that would have seemed grandiose just three years earlier: "a transformational year." The substance behind it was hard to argue. Vistra had closed on Energy Harbor, extended Comanche Peak's operating licences through 2050 and 2053, joined the S&P 500, and secured two large renewable PPAs with two of the world's most creditworthy corporate counterparties [Vistra FY2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2025-02-27-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2024-Results) [Vistra Comanche Peak renewal](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-07-30-Vistra-Receives-Approval-to-Operate-Comanche-Peak-Nuclear-Plant-Through-2053).

> "We've started construction on two new solar facilities, a 200 MW site backed by Amazon in Texas and a 405 MW site backed by Microsoft in Illinois."
> — Jim Burke, Q2 2024 earnings call, August 8, 2024

Those two sentences, tucked into an already eventful earnings release, marked Vistra's formal entry into the hyperscaler offtake business. The Microsoft deal — a long-term PPA for a 405 MW solar facility under development in Illinois — and the companion Amazon agreement for a 200 MW Texas solar project together totalled 605 MW of new contracted renewable capacity. Construction was under way on both as of Q1 2025, and by February 2026 management was also describing a separate 20-year AWS nuclear PPA at Comanche Peak [Vistra Q2 2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-08-08-Vistra-Reports-Second-Quarter-2024-Results) [Vistra FY2025 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-02-26-Vistra-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Results). No strike price or contract duration for the 2024 solar agreements was disclosed in SEC filings.

The solar agreements reflected the immediate contracting posture available in 2024: hyperscalers seeking to match their data-centre load growth with new clean electrons were constrained by what could be permitted, financed, and constructed within multi-year capital cycles. Utility-scale solar on previously coal-impacted land offered speed and regulatory clarity that nuclear relicensing and uprates could not match on the same timeline. But the solar PPAs proved to be a staging post rather than the endpoint for a company that, by 2026, had also disclosed large nuclear contracts with AWS and Meta.

## A 6.4 GW Nuclear Fleet and Its Hyperscaler Potential

Vistra's nuclear portfolio — 2.4 GW Comanche Peak in Texas plus the four Energy Harbor reactors in Ohio and Pennsylvania totalling roughly 4 GW — generates electricity with a capacity factor consistently above 90 percent. For hyperscalers, that profile is as close to purpose-built power as the grid offers: always-on, carbon-free, not contingent on weather. The IRA's Section 45U production tax credit, which provides a floor on nuclear economics through a sliding-scale PTC tied to the prevailing power price, has further de-risked the assets and made long-term offtake pricing more tractable.

On the Q3 2024 earnings call, Burke indicated Vistra was "making progress" on plans to develop up to 2,000 MW of new dispatchable natural gas generation in ERCOT, conditional on market reform implementation and forward price trajectory. That framing — evaluating regulatory catalysts before committing capital — extends to nuclear offtake as well. On multiple earnings calls through 2024 and into 2025, the team signalled active discussions with additional hyperscalers about the nuclear fleet, without announcing specific counterparties or terms.

The Comanche Peak licence renewal, approved by the NRC through 2050 and 2053 for Units 1 and 2 respectively, removed a material uncertainty from any prospective long-term nuclear PPA. A 20-year agreement is easier to finance when the underlying plant has already been relicensed through mid-century rather than when it is still operating under original licences that would have expired in 2030 and 2033 [Vistra Comanche Peak renewal](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-07-30-Vistra-Receives-Approval-to-Operate-Comanche-Peak-Nuclear-Plant-Through-2053).

## TXU Energy: The Retail Anchor

Against this forward-looking hyperscaler narrative sat a business that had generated cash for more than two decades: TXU Energy, Vistra's Texas retail brand and one of the largest competitive electricity retailers in the state. TXU itself served approximately 2.6 million Texas customers as of year-end 2025, while Vistra's total retail book across 16 states and the District of Columbia served approximately 5 million customers [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm).

The retail segment generated $1,463 million in adjusted EBITDA for fiscal year 2024, up from $1,105 million in 2023 — a 32 percent increase reflecting both volume growth and improved margin management. The second quarter of 2024 was particularly striking: retail EBITDA reached $789 million in a single quarter, a figure Burke described as representing "retail performance levels not achieved in the more than two decades competitive markets have been open." In a year when the Texas wholesale market delivered its share of volatility, the ability of the integrated retail book to capture margin on that volatility — buying and selling around the TXU customer load — was the structural hedge working exactly as designed.

Vistra also operates Ambit Energy, the multi-state retail electricity and natural gas brand acquired in 2019, which extends competitive supply to customers in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, New York, and other deregulated states. The Energy Harbor acquisition added approximately one million additional retail customers in PJM markets, predominantly in Ohio and Pennsylvania, deepening the retail book outside Texas for the first time at scale. Retail EBITDA from the East segment, which houses Energy Harbor's contribution, reached $2,017 million in fiscal 2024 — effectively matching the Texas segment's $2,032 million, reflecting the transformation in Vistra's geographic earnings mix.

## Wholesale Market Exposure

The remainder of Vistra's generation output sells through the five ISO/RTO markets where it operates: ERCOT, PJM, MISO, NYISO, and ISO-NE. Each market has its own capacity construct, energy price formation mechanism, and ancillary services stack, and Vistra manages a sophisticated commercial hedging programme across all of them.

The hedging posture remained consistently aggressive. As of August 5, 2024, Vistra said it had hedged approximately 94 percent of expected generation volumes for the balance of 2024, 86 percent for 2025 and 55 percent for 2026. By May 1, 2026, after Energy Harbor and Lotus were fully inside the fleet, the company said it had hedged approximately 98 percent of expected 2026 generation, 89 percent for 2027 and 65 percent for 2028 [Vistra Q2 2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-08-08-Vistra-Reports-Second-Quarter-2024-Results) [Vistra Q1 2026 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-05-07-Vistra-Reports-First-Quarter-2026-Results). PJM's 2025/26 capacity auction, which cleared at dramatically elevated prices in July 2024, materially improved the revenue outlook for Energy Harbor's Ohio and Pennsylvania fleet.

## Natural Gas: Flexible Backbone and Supply Chain

Natural gas-fired generation remained the largest share of Vistra's installed capacity. The company's 2025 10-K showed a 43,641 MW total fleet after the Lotus acquisition, with natural gas still the dominant fuel category and Lotus alone adding 2,557 MW in PJM, ISO-NE, NYISO and CAISO [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm). The gas book spans combined-cycle plants optimised for baseload-adjacent running and simple-cycle peakers designed to capture scarcity pricing during demand spikes. In ERCOT, where there is no formal capacity market, peaker margin remained highly correlated with weather extremes.

Natural gas supply is contracted through a combination of Henry Hub-indexed physical supply agreements and regional basis hedges, with pipeline transportation agreements covering delivery to individual plant gates. Vistra does not operate upstream gas assets, making it a price-taker at Henry Hub and at regional basis differentials — a structure that keeps the balance sheet clean but leaves earnings exposed to regional gas price dislocations, particularly the Waha Hub basis blow-outs that have periodically flipped west Texas gas prices negative.

Vistra's response to the structural demand signal from ERCOT — AI data-centre load, electrification of industrial processes, and population growth — was a stated commitment to add up to 2,000 MW of new dispatchable gas in Texas, contingent on market-reform signals. In May 2025, Vistra also moved decisively in the broader merchant gas market, agreeing to acquire about 2,600 MW of modern combined-cycle and combustion-turbine capacity from Lotus Infrastructure Partners for roughly $1.9 billion [Vistra Q2 2024 results](https://investor.vistracorp.com/2024-08-08-Vistra-Reports-Second-Quarter-2024-Results) [Vistra Lotus announcement](https://investor.vistracorp.com/news?o=30).

> "We believe natural gas fired generation will continue to play an ever-increasing role in the reliability, affordability, and flexibility of U.S. power grids for years to come."
> — Jim Burke, May 2025

The Lotus deal, priced at approximately $743 per kilowatt, extended Vistra's gas presence into markets where it had previously been modest, deepening the multi-ISO earnings diversification the Energy Harbor acquisition had begun [Vistra Lotus announcement](https://investor.vistracorp.com/news?o=30).

## The Uranium Supply Chain

For a merchant generator, nuclear fuel cycle supply chain management is among the most operationally consequential tasks that never appears on a headline earnings slide. Vistra's 6.4 GW nuclear fleet requires a continuous pipeline of uranium concentrate, conversion services, enrichment, and fuel fabrication — each representing a distinct supply market with its own geopolitical exposure.

Public disclosures were more guarded on nuclear-fuel counterparties than they were on duration. In its 2025 Form 10-K, Vistra said it had nuclear fuel contracted to support all of its refuelling needs through 2030 and did not anticipate significant difficulties in acquiring uranium or contracting for associated conversion, enrichment and fabrication services [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm). That still left the underlying commercial reality intact: nuclear-fuel procurement had become a far more important supply-chain competency after the Energy Harbor acquisition expanded the fleet from one plant to six operating reactors.

The IRA's Section 45U production tax credit, active from 2024 through 2032, placed a statutory floor under nuclear economics when wholesale power prices weakened. That floor reduced the urgency of locking every megawatt-hour into whatever bilateral price the market would bear in a given month, providing Vistra's commercial team more room to pursue hyperscaler-grade structures that reflected the scarcity value of always-on zero-carbon capacity [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm).

Coal supply, once a major procurement consideration for Vistra's legacy Illinois and Ohio plants, has diminished substantially as the coal retirement programme advances. The Illinois Coal-to-Solar conversions at Baldwin and Coffeen — which brought 70 MW and 46 MW of solar-plus-storage online in 2024 — are the visible expression of that transition, converting stranded land and grid interconnection rights into renewable generation infrastructure that can support new offtake agreements.

chapters.title: Where Vistra sits against Constellation, NRG, NextEra, and Talen
chapters.body:
## A Market Reshaped

The map changed again when Constellation completed its acquisition of Calpine on 7 January 2026. With 55 GW of capacity, the combined group became the nation's largest producer of electricity, leaving Vistra as the clearest number-two merchant competitor with 43,641 MW of capacity at year-end 2025. Standing second in that hierarchy was still strategically meaningful: Vistra's moat lay in ERCOT depth, retail integration through TXU Energy, and a 6,448 MW nuclear fleet that could be sold into the same AI-driven power market Constellation and Talen were targeting [Constellation completes Calpine](https://www.constellationenergy.com/newsroom/2026/01/constellation-completes-calpine-transaction-powering-americas-clean-energy-future.html) [Vistra 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000169281926000006/vistra-20251231.htm).

## Constellation: The Nuclear Benchmark

No peer comparison begins honestly without a clear-eyed accounting of the scale gap between Vistra and its principal comparable. Before absorbing Calpine, Constellation operated about 22 GW of nuclear capacity — the largest nuclear fleet in the United States and roughly 3.4 times Vistra's post-Energy-Harbor portfolio.
